items.name: SQL vs NoSQL
items.guide: Relational systems provide declarative queries and transactional constraints; non-relational systems span several distinct models rather than one SQL-free category. Compare invariants, query patterns, consistency, schema evolution, and operating expertise.

items.name: B-tree vs LSM-tree
items.guide: B-trees support ordered lookup and updates through page-oriented structures; LSM designs buffer and merge writes across sorted runs, trading write behavior against compaction, read amplification, and space amplification. Actual engines combine techniques.

items.name: Range vs hash vs consistent-hash vs directory partitioning
items.guide: Range placement supports ordered scans but can create skew; hash placement spreads keys but weakens range locality; consistent hashing can limit remapping when membership changes; directory placement adds a lookup/control layer and can route flexibly at that layer's availability and scale cost.

items.name: Normalization vs denormalization
items.guide: Normalization reduces duplicated facts and update anomalies; denormalization can reduce read joins or distribute precomputed views while adding write coordination, freshness, storage, and repair work.

items.name: ACID vs BASE
items.guide: ACID names transaction properties; BASE is an informal family of availability-oriented, eventually convergent design choices, not a formal opposite protocol. Compare concrete transaction and consistency guarantees for each operation.

items.name: Strong vs eventual consistency
items.guide: Specify the actual consistency model and operation. Linearizable reads/writes give stronger ordering than eventual convergence but can require coordination; eventual consistency alone gives no fixed freshness bound.

items.name: CAP and PACELC applied
items.guide: CAP concerns atomic consistency (linearizable behavior) and availability during a network partition under its model; PACELC also highlights latency-versus-consistency choices when there is no partition. These are reasoning lenses, not database product labels.

items.name: Leader-follower vs multi-leader vs leaderless replication
items.guide: A leader can simplify write order but creates election/failover dependencies; multi-leader permits concurrent writes and requires conflict policy; leaderless designs use replica protocols and quorum assumptions. Compare topology, consistency, failure, and repair behavior.

items.name: 2PC vs saga vs TCC
items.guide: Two-phase commit coordinates participants in one distributed transaction and may block while a decision is unresolved; a saga composes local transactions with compensations; Try-Confirm-Cancel reserves then commits or releases resources. None makes arbitrary external effects magically atomic.

items.name: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency control
items.guide: Optimistic control detects conflicts at validation/commit and suits workloads with tolerable retries; pessimistic control prevents some conflicts by locking but can block or deadlock. Choose from contention, transaction duration, and failure/retry semantics.

items.name: Latency vs throughput
items.guide: Latency is time for an operation; throughput is completed work per unit time. Concurrency and batching can increase throughput while raising queueing and tail latency. Measure distributions under representative load.

items.name: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
items.guide: Vertical scaling increases resources within a node and may simplify stateful operation until limits or failure concentration dominate; horizontal scaling adds nodes and requires distribution, coordination, and capacity management.

items.name: Cache-aside vs write-through vs write-behind
items.guide: Cache-aside loads on demand; write-through updates cache and backing store according to a policy; write-behind acknowledges before deferred persistence and therefore needs explicit durability, ordering, and loss/replay handling.

items.name: Token bucket vs sliding-window rate limiting
items.guide: Token bucket bounds sustained rate while allowing configured bursts; sliding-window approaches measure activity over a moving interval with implementation choices for exactness and cost. Distributed enforcement adds synchronization or approximation tradeoffs.

items.name: Single-region vs multi-region deployment
items.guide: One region reduces cross-region complexity but leaves regional recovery requirements; multiple regions can reduce locality or recovery time for some users while introducing replication lag, conflict, failover, cost, and residency decisions.

items.name: Monolith vs microservices
items.guide: A modular monolith has one deployable application boundary with internal modules; microservices introduce independently deployable network boundaries, ownership and failure isolation alongside contract, operations, latency, and data-consistency costs.

items.name: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL
items.guide: REST is an architectural style; HTTP APIs commonly use resource-oriented semantics. gRPC defines service contracts and its mainstream RPC protocol uses HTTP/2. GraphQL lets clients select fields through a schema and server execution. Evaluate browser/client constraints, evolution, caching, tooling, streaming, and operational policy.

items.name: Load balancer vs reverse proxy vs API gateway
items.guide: A load balancer distributes traffic; a reverse proxy receives and forwards requests; an API gateway applies API-level routing and policy. Products may combine roles, so compare the responsibilities and failure domain rather than names alone.

items.name: Batch vs stream processing
items.guide: Batch computes over bounded or accumulated data; stream processing handles continuing events with explicit event time, state, lateness, and recovery semantics. Many systems combine both.

items.name: Lambda vs Kappa architecture
items.guide: Lambda separates batch and stream paths and reconciles their views; Kappa favors a replayable stream-processing path. They differ in code paths, replay capability, historical recomputation, and operational burden, not simply speed.

items.name: Polling vs long-polling vs SSE vs WebSockets vs webhooks
items.guide: Polling is client initiated on intervals; long-polling holds a request until data or timeout; SSE is one-way server-to-client over HTTP; WebSockets are bidirectional; webhooks deliver server-to-server callbacks. Choose by direction, latency, connectivity, replay, scale, and authentication needs.

items.name: Push vs pull delivery and fan-out
items.guide: Push distributes work/data to consumers proactively and can create hot consumers or fan-out bursts; pull lets consumers control pace but adds polling delay and cursor/lease management. Hybrid systems partition responsibility and need backpressure.
